# Introduction

This exercise utilizes the [suburban Cook County Health Atlas](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org) and [Chicago Health Atlas](https://chicagohealthatlas.org) indicators to evaluate select public health outcomes relative to transportation access and quality across Cook County. The exercise will make use of indicators derived from local surveys (i.e., [Cook County Health Survey](https://cookcountypublichealth.org/health-survey/) and the [Healthy Chicago Survey](https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/cdph/supp_info/healthy-communities/healthy-chicago-survey.html)) that are administered annually by the two local health departments. Both surveys are designed to collect neighborhood-level information from residents on such things as health status, risk behaviors, and access to health care to inform and monitor the health status of communities. [Download the exercise #4 presentation](https://justenvirons.org/pedagogy/GEO330/Exercise_04/slides/Exercise04_Template.pptx) template to organize data elements and summaries. Submit the completed presentation to the appropriate submission folder on D2L.

# Step 2. Create health and transportation indicator dataset

## Combine countywide geographies
Health indicators on the Chicago atlas are reported by community area, whereas those on the suburban Cook County atlas are reported by municipality. To map and compare indicators across the county, the two have been combined into a novel geography (`novel_geo_cook`, N=202) of city of Chicago community areas (N=77) and suburban Cook County municipalities of at least 4 square miles (N=125), using GeoJSON data imported from the two health atlases. The geography was loaded in Step 1; the function used to create it is shown below for reference. @tbl-novel_geo summarizes the areas in the new geography.

```{r}
#| label: define county-wide geography functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the county-wide geography functions"

# function for combining Chicago community areas and suburban Cook County
# municipalities of at least min_sqmi square miles into a single county-wide
# ("novel") geography; community area geoids drop the Chicago place prefix
# ("1714000-") so they match the indicator data
fx_create_novel_geo <- function(community_areas, places_cook_county, min_sqmi = 4) {
  community_areas <- community_areas %>%
    transmute(geoid = str_replace(id, "^1714000-", ""),
              name,
              location = "Chicago, IL",
              type = "community area")

  places_cook_county <- places_cook_county %>%
    mutate(sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) * 0.0000003861) %>%
    filter(sqmi >= min_sqmi) %>%
    transmute(geoid = id,
              name,
              location = "suburban Cook County",
              type = "municipality")

  bind_rows(places_cook_county, community_areas) %>%
    st_make_valid()
}

# function for summarizing the county-wide geography by type: number of areas
# and total, smallest and largest areas (square miles)
fx_table_novel_geo <- function(novel_geo_cook) {
  novel_geo_cook %>%
    mutate(sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(st_transform(geometry, 3435))) * 0.0000003861) %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    group_by(location, type) %>%
    summarise(areas = n(),
              sqmi_total = sum(sqmi),
              sqmi_min = min(sqmi),
              sqmi_max = max(sqmi),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    datatable(class = 'cell-border stripe',
              selection = "none",
              rownames = FALSE,
              colnames = c("Location", "Type", "Areas", "Total Square Miles",
                           "Smallest (Square Miles)", "Largest (Square Miles)"),
              options = list(searching = FALSE, lengthChange = FALSE, paging = FALSE)) %>%
    formatRound(c("sqmi_total", "sqmi_min", "sqmi_max"), digits = 1)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-novel_geo
#| tbl-cap: Novel Cook County Geography by Location and Type

# summarize the county-wide geography
fx_table_novel_geo(novel_geo_cook)

```

## Merge select suburban Cook County and city of Chicago indicators

The next step is to download and merge similar indicator data from the two atlases for statistical analysis and mapping. Both suburban Cook County and the city of Chicago regularly survey their residents about health. Indicators derived from these surveys are shared on the atlases. Many indicators on the two atlases are aligned so that they can be compared across jurisdictions, including those below.

The selected health survey indicators, which are comparable across both atlases, were downloaded and combined for you and loaded in Step 1 (`indicators_all`). @tbl-health_indicators lists each indicator's column name, its topic keys and the survey periods used for each jurisdiction. Below are links to each jurisdiction's charts and thematic maps for the selected indicators. Before running any statistics, review the indicators and form your own hypotheses about how they relate to one another and to active transportation: walking, bicycling, and public transit use.

-   Adult obesity rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8YZKL) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSOBP))
-   Neighborhood safety rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8SRFE) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSNSP))
-   Neighborhood sidewalk quality rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8IQGF) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSNSQP))
-   Neighborhood ambulatory difficulty rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/AMBDHSR) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSIDQZ))
-   Ease of walking to transit stop rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8OWII) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSWTSP))
-   Overall health status ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8OLNB) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSOHSP))
-   Physical inactivity rate ([SCC](https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/JG8MIQE) \| [Chicago](https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/HCSPAP))

On **slide 1** of your presentation, speculate about the relationships between **two or more** of these indicators and how they may encourage or discourage active transportation. For each relationship you propose:

1.  **State the relationship and its expected direction.** For example, communities with higher physical inactivity rates may also report poorer overall health status, or places with better sidewalk quality may report easier walking access to transit stops.
2.  **Explain the mechanism.** Why might these indicators move together? Consider the built environment (sidewalks, transit access), perceptions (neighborhood safety), and individual capacity (ambulatory difficulty, obesity, overall health).
3.  **Connect it to walking, bicycling, and/or transit use.** For example, does feeling unsafe in a neighborhood discourage walking to a bus stop at night? Can poor sidewalks turn a short walk to transit into a barrier for someone with ambulatory difficulty?
4.  **Consider the direction of causality.** Does poor health lead to less walking and cycling, or does an environment that discourages active travel lead to poorer health? Could both be true, or could a third factor (e.g., income, car ownership, land use) explain both?
5.  **Anticipate geographic differences.** Would you expect these relationships to look the same in Chicago and suburban Cook County? Why or why not?

You will test these hypotheses with the merged data in the steps that follow, so treat this slide as a set of predictions that you will revisit.

```{r}
#| label: define indicator download functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the indicator download functions"

# function for downloading one health survey indicator from one atlas ("scc" for
# suburban Cook County municipalities or "chicago" for Chicago community areas);
# key is the atlas topic key, period the survey period and column the indicator's
# (one word) column name. Chicago results also include other cities, so only
# community areas are kept, and their geoids drop the Chicago place prefix.
fx_read_atlas_indicator <- function(atlas, key, period, column, read = jsonlite::fromJSON) {
  results <- read(sprintf(atlas_urls[[atlas]], period, key))$results %>%
    as.data.frame()
  if (atlas == "chicago") results <- filter(results, str_starts(g, "1714000-"))

  results %>%
    transmute(geoid = str_replace(g, "^1714000-", ""),
              atlas = !!atlas,
              topic = !!column,
              estimate = as.numeric(v),
              se = if ("se" %in% names(results)) as.numeric(se) else NA_real_)
}

# function for downloading every indicator in the indicators table (columns
# column, scc_key, scc_period, chicago_key and chicago_period) from both atlases
# and combining them into one long table (one row per area and indicator)
fx_download_indicators <- function(indicators, read = jsonlite::fromJSON) {
  bind_rows(
    pmap(list(indicators$scc_key, indicators$scc_period, indicators$column),
         function(key, period, column) fx_read_atlas_indicator("scc", key, period, column, read)),
    pmap(list(indicators$chicago_key, indicators$chicago_period, indicators$column),
         function(key, period, column) fx_read_atlas_indicator("chicago", key, period, column, read)))
}

# function for formatting the indicators table, with links to each indicator's
# page on the two atlases
fx_table_health_indicators <- function(indicators) {
  indicators %>%
    mutate(scc_key = sprintf('<a href="https://cookcountyhealthatlas.org/indicators/%s" target="_blank">%s</a>', scc_key, scc_key),
           chicago_key = sprintf('<a href="https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/%s" target="_blank">%s</a>', chicago_key, chicago_key)) %>%
    datatable(class = 'cell-border stripe',
              selection = "none",
              rownames = FALSE,
              escape = FALSE,
              colnames = c("Column", "Indicator", "SCC Key", "SCC Period", "Chicago Key", "Chicago Period"),
              options = list(searching = FALSE, lengthChange = FALSE, paging = FALSE))
}
```

To swap in different indicators later, edit the topic keys and periods in `health_indicators` (use the links above, or the atlases' data dictionaries, to find them) and download the indicators again with the code below. The download takes a minute or so. *Optional: you do not need to run this code to complete the exercise.*

# Step 3. Map and explore indicators

## Join indicator attributes with county-wide geographies

Next, use the code below to join the indicator attributes to the county-wide geography layer. The result (`indicators_geo`) is a spatially enabled table, with one row per area and one column per indicator, that you will use to make custom maps in the steps that follow. @tbl-indicators shows the joined indicators; click a column name to sort the table, or type in the boxes below the column names to filter it.

```{r}
#| label: define indicator join and table functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the indicator join and table functions"

# function for joining the downloaded indicators (one column per indicator, plus
# its standard error, se_<column>) to the county-wide geography; areas without
# indicator data are left out
fx_join_indicators <- function(indicators_all, novel_geo_cook) {
  indicators_wide <- indicators_all %>%
    pivot_wider(id_cols = c(geoid, atlas),
                names_from = topic,
                values_from = c(estimate, se)) %>%
    rename_with(~ str_remove(.x, "^estimate_"))

  novel_geo_cook %>%
    inner_join(indicators_wide, by = "geoid") %>%
    st_as_sf()
}

# function for formatting the joined indicators as an interactive table that can
# be sorted (click a column name) and filtered (boxes under the column names)
fx_table_indicators <- function(indicators_geo, indicators = health_indicators) {
  indicators <- filter(indicators, column %in% names(indicators_geo))
  indicators_geo %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(name, type, all_of(indicators$column)) %>%
    arrange(type, name) %>%
    datatable(class = 'cell-border stripe',
              selection = "none",
              rownames = FALSE,
              filter = "top",
              colnames = c("Name", "Type", indicators$name),
              options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)) %>%
    formatRound(indicators$column, digits = 1)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-indicators
#| tbl-cap: Health Survey Indicators by Chicago Community Area and Suburban Cook County Municipality

# join indicators to the county-wide geography
indicators_geo <- fx_join_indicators(indicators_all, novel_geo_cook)

# show the joined indicators
fx_table_indicators(indicators_geo, health_indicators)

```

## Create univariate maps of select indicators

Before measuring how indicators relate to one another, look at each indicator on its own. A univariate map shows one variable at a time and answers a simple question: *where* are rates high or low? It's easier to read correlations and bivariate maps once you know how each variable is distributed across the county.

@fig-communityarea_sccplaces is an interactive map of the new geography (`novel_geo_cook`). It combines suburban Cook County municipalities (dark gray border) and Chicago community areas (light gray border), with the merged indicators attached. Choose an indicator from the "Indicator" dropdown list in the upper right of the map to display it as a thematic map, grouped into quintiles (each about 20 percent of places); places without data for the selected indicator are shown in light gray. The city of Chicago boundary (dashed black line) and Cook County boundary (dark red line) make it easier to see where Chicago ends and suburban Cook County begins. Hover over or click individual places to see their values for every indicator. Change the color palette in the code below ([see this reference for palette names](https://i0.wp.com/1.bp.blogspot.com/-3VQwNXWga9s/UICXF7rbvLI/AAAAAAAAAUg/UQBmpUO9kVA/s1600/display-brewer-all.png)) to create a custom version of the map.

Explore **at least two** of the indicators you discussed on slide 1. For each one, consider:

1.  **Overall pattern.** Are high and low rates clustered in certain parts of the county (e.g., the North Shore, the south suburbs, Chicago's South and West Sides, the downtown core)? Or are they scattered?
2.  **Extremes and outliers.** Which places have the highest and lowest rates? Do any places stand out sharply from their neighbors?
3.  **City–suburb boundary.** Do rates change abruptly at the Chicago city limits? If they do, think about whether that reflects real differences between places or differences in how the two jurisdictions run their surveys, word their questions, or estimate rates for small areas.
4.  **Missing or unreliable data.** Are any places blank or flagged? How might gaps affect what you conclude?
5.  **Comparison with your predictions.** Does the pattern match what you expected on slide 1? What surprised you, and what might explain it?

On **slides 2 and 3** of your presentation, paste one univariate map per slide, each showing a different indicator. Under each map, write 2–3 sentences that:

-   describe where rates are higher and lower,
-   point out at least one specific place or cluster that stands out, and
-   note whether the pattern supports, contradicts, or complicates the relationship you proposed on slide 1.

Then compare your two maps. Do high (or low) values of the two indicators seem to show up in the same places? Note your impressions. You'll test them formally with correlations and bivariate maps in the next step.

```{r}
#| label: define indicator mapping functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the indicator mapping functions"

# function for creating the base map shared by the exercise's interactive maps:
# CARTO basemap and reset and full screen buttons
fx_basemap <- function(map_data, carto_api_key = CARTO_API_KEY) {
  leaflet(data = st_transform(map_data, crs = 4326)) %>%
    addTiles(urlTemplate = paste0(
      "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/rastertiles/light_all/{z}/{x}/{y}.png?key=",
      carto_api_key
    )) %>%
    addResetMapButton() %>%
    addFullscreenControl()
}

# function for creating a quintile color palette; when repeated values make some
# quintile breaks identical, the remaining distinct breaks are used instead.
# Areas without data are shown in light grey.
fx_quintile_pal <- function(values, palette = "YlGnBu") {
  breaks <- unique(quantile(values, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2), na.rm = TRUE))
  if (length(breaks) < 2) breaks <- c(breaks, breaks + 1)
  colorBin(palette = palette, domain = values, bins = breaks, na.color = "#e0e0e0")
}

# function for formatting legend values (quintile ranges) to one decimal place
fx_legend_format <- function(type, cuts, p) {
  values <- formatC(cuts, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
  paste0(values[-length(values)], " &ndash; ", values[-1])
}

# function for creating hover (and click) labels with each area's name, geoid,
# type and location, and its value for every indicator ("no data" when missing)
fx_indicator_labels <- function(map_data, indicators = health_indicators) {
  values <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(indicators)), function(i) {
    x <- map_data[[indicators$column[i]]]
    sprintf("<i>%s:</i> %s<br/>",
            indicators$name[i],
            ifelse(is.na(x), "no data", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)))
  })
  values <- matrix(values, nrow = nrow(map_data))
  paste0("<strong>", map_data$name, "</strong><br/>",
         "<i>geoid:</i> ", map_data$geoid, "<br/>",
         "<i>type:</i> ", map_data$type, "<br/>",
         "<i>location:</i> ", map_data$location, "<hr style='margin: 3px 0;'/>",
         apply(values, 1, paste, collapse = ""))
}

# function for adding the city of Chicago (dashed black line) and Cook County
# (dark red line) boundaries; they are drawn above the other layers in their own
# pane and do not respond to the mouse, so the hover labels beneath them work
fx_add_boundaries <- function(map, chicago_boundary, cook_county_boundary) {
  map %>%
    addMapPane("boundaries", zIndex = 450) %>%
    addPolygons(
      data = st_transform(cook_county_boundary, crs = 4326),
      fill = FALSE,
      color = "#7a0019",
      weight = 3,
      opacity = 0.9,
      options = pathOptions(pane = "boundaries", interactive = FALSE)) %>%
    addPolygons(
      data = st_transform(chicago_boundary, crs = 4326),
      fill = FALSE,
      color = "#000000",
      weight = 2.5,
      opacity = 0.9,
      dashArray = "6 4",
      options = pathOptions(pane = "boundaries", interactive = FALSE))
}

# function for adding a dropdown list (top right) that shows one map layer (and
# its legend) at a time; groups are the layers' group names, in dropdown order,
# and each layer's legend carries the class "indicator-legend-<position in
# groups, from 0>". The layer at position selected (from 0) is shown first.
fx_add_layer_dropdown <- function(map, groups, selected = 0) {
  map %>%
    htmlwidgets::onRender("
      function(el, x, data) {
        var map = this;
        var groups = [].concat(data.groups);
        // show the selected layer and legend and hide the others
        function show(i) {
          groups.forEach(function(g, j) {
            var layer = map.layerManager.getLayerGroup(g, false);
            if (layer) { if (j === i) { map.addLayer(layer); } else { map.removeLayer(layer); } }
          });
          el.querySelectorAll('.indicator-legend').forEach(function(d) {
            d.style.display = d.classList.contains('indicator-legend-' + i) ? '' : 'none';
          });
        }
        var control = L.control({position: 'topright'});
        control.onAdd = function() {
          var div = L.DomUtil.create('div', 'leaflet-bar');
          div.style.background = 'white';
          div.style.padding = '4px 6px';
          div.innerHTML = '<label style=\"font-weight: bold; margin-right: 4px;\">Indicator</label>';
          var select = L.DomUtil.create('select', '', div);
          groups.forEach(function(g, j) {
            var option = L.DomUtil.create('option', '', select);
            option.value = j;
            option.text = g;
          });
          select.value = data.selected;
          select.onchange = function() { show(parseInt(select.value)); };
          L.DomEvent.disableClickPropagation(div);
          L.DomEvent.disableScrollPropagation(div);
          return div;
        };
        control.addTo(map);
        show(data.selected);
      }", data = list(groups = groups, selected = selected))
}

# function for mapping the county-wide geography with a dropdown list of the
# indicators in indicators_geo, each grouped into quintiles (the first indicator
# is shown when the map opens; "None" shows only the geography). Community areas
# have light grey borders and municipalities dark grey borders, and the city of
# Chicago and Cook County boundaries are drawn on top. palette is any
# RColorBrewer palette name (e.g., "YlGnBu", "Purples", "Greys")
fx_map_indicators <- function(novel_geo_cook, indicators_geo, chicago_boundary, cook_county_boundary,
                              indicators = health_indicators, palette = "YlGnBu") {
  indicators <- filter(indicators, column %in% names(indicators_geo))

  # all county-wide areas, with indicator values attached
  map_data <- novel_geo_cook %>%
    left_join(indicators_geo %>%
                st_drop_geometry() %>%
                select(geoid, all_of(indicators$column)),
              by = "geoid") %>%
    st_transform(crs = 4326)

  labels <- fx_indicator_labels(map_data, indicators)
  border_pal <- colorFactor(palette = c("lightgrey", "darkgrey"),
                            levels = c("community area", "municipality"))
  groups <- c("None (geography only)", indicators$name)

  # geography only
  map <- fx_basemap(map_data) %>%
    addPolygons(
      data = map_data,
      label = lapply(labels, htmltools::HTML),
      popup = labels,
      weight = 1,
      opacity = 1,
      color = border_pal(map_data$type),
      fillColor = "white",
      fillOpacity = 0.2,
      group = groups[1]) %>%
    addLegend("bottomright",
              colors = c("lightgrey", "darkgrey", "#000000", "#7a0019"),
              labels = c("Community area (Chicago)", "Municipality (suburban Cook County)",
                         "City of Chicago boundary", "Cook County boundary"),
              title = "Boundaries",
              opacity = 1)

  # one layer (and legend) per indicator, grouped into quintiles
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(indicators))) {
    values <- map_data[[indicators$column[i]]]
    if (all(is.na(values))) next # skip indicators without any data
    pal <- fx_quintile_pal(values, palette = palette)
    map <- map %>%
      addPolygons(
        data = map_data,
        label = lapply(labels, htmltools::HTML),
        popup = labels,
        weight = 1,
        opacity = 1,
        color = border_pal(map_data$type),
        fillColor = pal(values),
        fillOpacity = 0.7,
        group = groups[i + 1]) %>%
      addLegend("bottomleft",
                pal = pal,
                values = values,
                title = paste0(indicators$name[i], "<br/>(quintiles)"),
                labFormat = fx_legend_format,
                opacity = 0.7,
                className = paste0("info legend indicator-legend indicator-legend-", i))
  }

  map %>%
    fx_add_boundaries(chicago_boundary, cook_county_boundary) %>%
    fx_add_layer_dropdown(groups, selected = if (length(groups) > 1) 1 else 0)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-communityarea_sccplaces
#| fig-cap: Health Survey Indicators by Novel Cook County Geography (Quintiles)

                  indicators_geo,
                  chicago_boundary,
                  cook_county_boundary,
```

# Step 4. Examine statistical relationships between selected variables

Use the code below to create a bivariate correlation plot to explore the statistical relationships between the seven downloaded indicator variables (`indicators_geo`). Only areas with data for every indicator are included. Pearson's bivariate correlation (or Pearson's r) quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between each pair of variables. The coefficients range from -1 to +1 with values greater than 0 indicating positive linear relationships (i.e., as one variable increases, the other variable also increases) and values less than 0 indicating a negative linear relationship (i.e., as one variable increases, the other variable decreases). @fig-correlation_plots shows two plots based on the same correlation matrix: Plot 1 shows explicit correlation statistics and plot 2 shows graduated circles (larger circles for stronger relationships; black for negative and white for positive relationships). Indicators are ordered so that closely related indicators are next to each other. @tbl-correlations lists the same coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: define correlation functions
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the correlation functions"

# function for calculating Pearson's bivariate correlations between every pair of
# indicators; areas missing any indicator are left out
fx_correlations <- function(indicators_geo, indicators = health_indicators) {
  indicators_geo %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(any_of(indicators$column)) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    cor(method = "pearson")
}

# function for plotting a correlation matrix, with indicators ordered so that
# closely related indicators are next to each other; method is "number"
# (correlation coefficients) or "circle" (graduated circles)
fx_plot_correlations <- function(indicator_correlations, method = "number") {
  corrplot(indicator_correlations,
           method = method,
           col = c("black", "white"),
           order = "hclust",
           bg = "lightgrey",
           tl.col = "grey")
}

# function for formatting a correlation matrix as an interactive table
fx_table_correlations <- function(indicator_correlations) {
  indicator_correlations %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    rownames_to_column("indicator") %>%
    datatable(class = 'cell-border stripe',
              selection = "none",
              rownames = FALSE,
              colnames = c("Indicator" = "indicator"),
              options = list(searching = FALSE, lengthChange = FALSE, paging = FALSE)) %>%
    formatRound(rownames(indicator_correlations), digits = 2)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation_plots
#| fig-cap: Bivariate Correlation Plots (Pearson)
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Correlation coefficients"
#|   - "Graduated circles"
#| layout-ncol: 2

# calculate bivariate correlations between all indicators
indicator_correlations <- fx_correlations(indicators_geo, health_indicators)

# plot 1: correlation coefficients
fx_plot_correlations(indicator_correlations, method = "number")

# plot 2: graduated circles
fx_plot_correlations(indicator_correlations, method = "circle")

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlations
#| tbl-cap: Bivariate Correlation Coefficients (Pearson) Between Health Survey Indicators

# show the correlation coefficients
fx_table_correlations(indicator_correlations)

```

1.  **Strongest relationships.** Identify the two or three strongest positive and negative correlations. Report each coefficient (r) and describe its direction in plain language (e.g., "places with higher physical inactivity rates tend to report poorer overall health").
2.  **Weak or absent relationships.** Point out at least one pair of indicators with a weak relationship (r close to 0). Is that surprising?
3.  **Active transportation.** Focus on the transportation-related indicators (sidewalk quality, neighborhood safety, ease of walking to a transit stop). Which health outcomes are most closely related to them, and what might that mean for walking, bicycling, and transit use?
4.  **Revisit your predictions.** Compare the results with the hypotheses on slide 1 and the patterns in your univariate maps (slides 2 and 3). Which predictions were supported, which were not, and what might explain the differences?

# Step 5. Create two custom bivariate maps
A bivariate map shows two indicators at once. Each indicator is split into three categories (terciles: low, medium and high, each about a third of the areas mapped), and each area is colored by its combination of the two categories, for nine colors in all. Areas that are high on both indicators are shown in the darkest color, areas that are low on both in the lightest color, and areas that are high on one but low on the other in the colors at the opposite corners of the legend. Areas without data for either indicator are shown in light grey, and the dashed line marks the city of Chicago boundary. @fig-bivariate_maps shows two examples.

Adapt the code below (look for the `EDIT HERE` comments) to create two custom bivariate maps, each combining a health outcome with a transportation-related indicator. Choose pairs based on your hypotheses (slide 1) and the correlations in Step 4; optionally, change the palette (the list of palettes is in the bivariate mapping function). *Add your custom maps to slides 5 and 6 of your presentation and describe the spatial patterns you see in each map. Where do the two indicators coincide (high-high or low-low), and where do they diverge? Do the patterns differ between Chicago and suburban Cook County?*

```{r}
#| label: define bivariate mapping function
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the bivariate mapping function"

# function for mapping two indicators together (bivariate map) in three
# categories (terciles) each, with a legend; x and y are indicator columns and
# xlab and ylab label the legend. Areas without data are shown in light grey.
# palette is a biscale palette: "Bluegill", "BlueGold", "BlueOr", "BlueYl",
# "Brown"/"Brown2", "DkBlue"/"DkBlue2", "DkCyan"/"DkCyan2",
# "DkViolet"/"DkViolet2", "GrPink"/"GrPink2", "PinkGrn", "PurpleGrn" or "PurpleOr"
fx_map_bivariate <- function(indicators_geo, x, y, xlab = x, ylab = y, palette = "BlueGold",
                             chicago_boundary = NULL) {
  map_data <- indicators_geo %>%
    drop_na(all_of(c(x, y))) %>%
    bi_class(x = x, y = y, style = "quantile", dim = 3) # x and y are column names (strings)

  map <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = indicators_geo, fill = "grey90", color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    geom_sf(data = map_data,
            mapping = aes(fill = bi_class),
            color = "white",
            linewidth = 0.1,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
    bi_scale_fill(pal = palette, dim = 3) +
    bi_theme()

  # optional city of Chicago boundary (dashed black line)
  if (!is.null(chicago_boundary)) {
    map <- map + geom_sf(data = chicago_boundary, fill = NA, color = "black",
                         linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed")
  }

  legend <- bi_legend(pal = palette,
                      dim = 3,
                      xlab = paste("Higher", xlab),
                      ylab = paste("Higher", ylab),
                      size = 8)

  ggdraw() +
    draw_plot(map, 0, 0, 1, 1) +
    draw_plot(legend, 0.05, 0.05, 0.3, 0.3)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bivariate_maps
#| fig-cap: Bivariate Maps
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Overall health status by ease of walking to transit stop"
#|   - "Physical inactivity by neighborhood sidewalk quality"
#| layout-ncol: 2

# bivariate map 1
fx_map_bivariate(indicators_geo,
                 x = "health", # EDIT HERE
                 y = "transit", # EDIT HERE
                 xlab = "Health", # EDIT HERE
                 ylab = "Transit Access", # EDIT HERE
                 palette = "BlueGold",
                 chicago_boundary = chicago_boundary)

# bivariate map 2
fx_map_bivariate(indicators_geo,
                 x = "inactivity", # EDIT HERE
                 y = "sidewalk", # EDIT HERE
                 xlab = "Inactivity", # EDIT HERE
                 ylab = "Sidewalk Quality", # EDIT HERE
                 palette = "PurpleOr",
                 chicago_boundary = chicago_boundary)

```
